title: Knowledge Distillation: Teacher to Student
description: A large teacher model's soft outputs train a small student, transferring dark knowledge the hard labels lack. Temperature-scaled softmax reveals the teacher's uncertainty structure, which the student mimics. Distilled students routinely keep 95 percent of teacher accuracy at a tenth of the size.

demo.code:
import math
teacher = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]
T = 2.0
soft = [math.exp(x / T) for x in teacher]
s = sum(soft); soft = [x / s for x in soft]
print("teacher logits:", teacher)
print("soft targets (T=2):", [round(x, 3) for x in soft])

title: Magnitude Pruning with Fine-Tuning
description: Weights with the smallest absolute values are zeroed out, then the sparse model is fine-tuned to recover accuracy. Iterative pruning removes a little at a time, which preserves accuracy far better than one-shot pruning. Modern sparse formats turn the zeros into real speedups.

demo.code:
w = [0.8, 0.01, -0.5, 0.003, 1.2, -0.02]
thr = 0.05
pruned = [0.0 if abs(x) < thr else x for x in w]
print("before:", w)
print("after: ", pruned)
print("sparsity: %.0f%%" % (100 * pruned.count(0.0) / len(pruned)))

title: Quantization-Aware Training Transform
description: QAT inserts fake quantization nodes during training so the model learns weights that survive INT8 rounding. The transform converts a trained FP32 graph into a quantization-ready graph automatically. Models trained this way lose far less accuracy than post-training quantization on sensitive architectures.

demo.code:
w = [0.37, -0.82, 1.15]
scale = 0.01
fake_q = [round(x / scale) * scale for x in w]
print("weights:", w)
print("fake-quantized:", fake_q)
print("model trains through this rounding")

title: Net2Net Widening Transform
description: Net2Net widens layers while preserving the exact function the network computes, so the larger model starts exactly where the smaller one left off. Each neuron is split into copies with halved outgoing weights. Training continues from a strictly better starting point than random initialization.

demo.code:
w = [0.5, -0.3]
widened = []
for x in w:
    widened.extend([x, x])
out_w = [v / 2 for v in [0.5, 0.5, -0.3, -0.3]]
print("widened layer:", widened)
print("halved outputs keep function identical:", out_w)

title: Structural Reparameterization (RepVGG)
description: Multi-branch training-time blocks are mathematically fused into single convolutions for inference. The transform adds the branch kernels together after folding batch norms, producing one equivalent kernel. Training gets the optimization benefits of branches while inference pays for one convolution.

demo.code:
k3, k1, ident = 1.0, 0.5, 0.25
fused = k3 + k1 + ident
print("branch kernels:", k3, k1, ident)
print("fused single kernel:", fused)
print("outputs identical by linearity")

t: Channel Pruning via BN Scaling Factors
title: Channel Pruning via BN Scaling Factors
description: Batch-norm scaling factors indicate channel importance, so channels with near-zero gamma are pruned structurally. The transform removes whole channels rather than individual weights, which keeps the model dense and fast. A sparsity penalty on gamma during training makes the selection clean.

demo.code:
gamma = [0.9, 0.02, 0.7, 0.001, 0.5]
keep = [g > 0.05 for g in gamma]
print("gamma:", gamma)
print("kept channels:", [i for i, k in enumerate(keep) if k])
print("channels removed:", keep.count(False))

title: Attention Head Pruning
description: Many attention heads are redundant, so the transform scores heads by their contribution and drops the weakest. Dropping whole heads shrinks both compute and the KV cache. Large transformers commonly lose a third of their heads with negligible quality change.

demo.code:
importance = [0.9, 0.1, 0.7, 0.05, 0.6, 0.02]
keep = [i for i, v in enumerate(importance) if v > 0.2]
print("head importance:", importance)
print("kept heads:", keep, "(%d/%d)" % (len(keep), len(importance)))

title: Layer Dropping (LayerDrop)
description: LayerDrop trains with random layers skipped, which makes the network robust to removing layers at inference. The transform then drops the least important layers for a smaller, faster model. Depth becomes a runtime knob rather than a fixed property.

demo.code:
layers = list(range(12))
importance = [0.9, 0.3, 0.8, 0.2, 0.7, 0.85, 0.1, 0.75, 0.6, 0.05, 0.65, 0.55]
drop = sorted(range(len(layers)), key=lambda i: importance[i])[:4]
kept = [l for l in layers if l not in drop]
print("dropped layers:", sorted(drop))
print("kept:", kept)

title: Progressive Shrinking (Once-for-All)
description: Once-for-All trains a supernet containing many sub-architectures, then extracts specialized subnets without retraining. The transform samples a subnet matching the deployment budget and calibrates its batch norms. One training run serves every device tier.

title: Depth-to-Width Reshaping
description: Some hardware prefers wide shallow graphs over narrow deep ones, so the transform redistributes capacity from depth to width while preserving parameter count. Function is approximately preserved through careful initialization of the reshaped layers. The reshaped model better matches the target accelerator's parallelism.

title: Self-Distillation (Born-Again Networks)
description: A model distills from itself: the trained model becomes the teacher for a fresh student of identical architecture. The student consistently beats the original, and the process can repeat for multiple generations. The gains come from the softened targets regularizing training.

demo.code:
gen = [81.2, 82.5, 83.1, 83.4]
for i, acc in enumerate(gen):
    print("generation %d accuracy: %.1f" % (i, acc))
print("total gain: +%.1f" % (gen[-1] - gen[0]))

title: Low-Rank Factorization of Layers
description: Dense layers are replaced by two smaller low-rank factors, cutting parameters from m*n to r*(m+n). The transform initializes factors from the SVD of the trained weights. Rank is chosen per layer by the singular value spectrum to bound the approximation error.

demo.code:
m, n, r = 1024, 1024, 64
before = m * n
after = r * (m + n)
print("params before: %d after: %d (%.1fx smaller)" % (before, after, before / after))

title: Dynamic Sparse Training (RigL)
description: RigL trains sparse from scratch, periodically dropping weak connections and regrowing promising ones. The transform keeps sparsity constant while the topology evolves. Final accuracy rivals dense training with a fraction of the FLOPs throughout.

demo.code:
sparsity, steps = 0.9, 5
for s in range(steps):
    print("step %d: drop weakest 10%%, regrow by gradient -> sparsity stays %.0f%%" % (s, 100 * sparsity))
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'RigL', 'transform_type': 'Dynamic sparsity', 'input_arch': 'Dense init', 'output_arch': 'Sparse trained', 'benefit': 'Sparse training, dense accuracy', 'complexity': 'High'}
print("technique:", _jah_schema["technique"])
assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'transform_type', 'input_arch', 'output_arch', 'benefit', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: Mixed-Precision Architecture Search
description: The transform searches per-layer bit widths jointly with the architecture, using a differentiable precision gate. Layers that tolerate quantization go to INT8 while sensitive layers stay FP16. The search optimizes accuracy per joule rather than accuracy alone.

demo.code:
layers = ["conv1", "conv2", "fc"]
choice = {"conv1": "int8", "conv2": "int8", "fc": "fp16"}
print("per-layer precision:", choice)
print("int8 layers:", sum(1 for v in choice.values() if v == "int8"))

title: Neural Architecture Morphism Operators
description: Morphism operators like widening, deepening, and skip-insertion change architecture while preserving the function exactly. NAS uses them to explore without retraining from scratch at each step. The morphism history also documents how the final architecture was found.

demo.code:
ops = ["widen", "deepen", "skip-insert"]
arch = "base"
for op in ops:
    arch += "+" + op
    print("apply", op, "->", arch)

title: Token Pruning for Transformers
description: Uninformative tokens are dropped as they flow through transformer layers, shrinking sequence length dynamically. The transform scores tokens by attention mass and keeps the top fraction per layer. Throughput rises because attention is quadratic in the tokens that remain.

demo.code:
tokens, keep_ratio = 512, 0.5
kept = int(tokens * keep_ratio)
print("tokens: %d -> %d" % (tokens, kept))
print("attention work: %.2fx less" % ((tokens / kept) ** 2))

title: Weight Sharing Across Layers (ALBERT)
description: Layers share one set of weights, so a 24-layer model carries the parameters of one layer. The transform ties the weights and trains with the sharing in place. Memory for parameters collapses while depth still adds representational power.

demo.code:
layers, per_layer = 24, 10_000_000
print("before: %d params" % (layers * per_layer))
print("after sharing: %d params" % per_layer)
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'Cross-layer sharing', 'transform_type': 'Sharing', 'input_arch': '24-layer model', 'output_arch': 'Shared-weight model', 'benefit': '24x fewer parameters', 'complexity': 'Medium'}
print("technique:", _jah_schema["technique"])
assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'transform_type', 'input_arch', 'output_arch', 'benefit', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: Early-Exit Branch Insertion
description: Classification heads are attached at intermediate layers so easy inputs exit early. The transform trains the exits jointly with a weighted loss. Average latency drops because most inputs never reach the final layer.

demo.code:
exits = [(4, 0.6), (8, 0.3), (12, 0.1)]
avg = sum(l * p for l, p in exits)
print("exit distribution:", exits)
print("average layers executed: %.1f of 12" % avg)

title: Sparse-to-Dense Distillation Recovery
description: After aggressive pruning, a dense teacher distills the sparse student back toward full accuracy. The transform pairs the pruned architecture with the original as teacher. Recovery usually closes most of the pruning gap within a short fine-tune.

demo.code:
acc = {"dense": 90.0, "pruned": 84.2, "distilled": 89.1}
print(acc)
print("gap closed: %.0f%%" % (100 * (acc["distilled"] - acc["pruned"]) / (acc["dense"] - acc["pruned"])))
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'Prune-then-distill', 'transform_type': 'Recovery', 'input_arch': 'Pruned student', 'output_arch': 'Recovered sparse model', 'benefit': 'Closes pruning gap', 'complexity': 'Medium'}
print("technique:", _jah_schema["technique"])
assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'transform_type', 'input_arch', 'output_arch', 'benefit', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: Block Floating Point Transform
description: BFP shares one exponent across a block of values, giving near-FP accuracy with integer-like hardware. The transform groups activations into blocks and picks per-block exponents. It is the precision format behind several efficient training systems.

demo.code:
block = [0.37, 1.42, 0.05, 2.71]
import math
exp = math.ceil(math.log2(max(abs(x) for x in block))) if max(abs(x) for x in block) > 0 else 0
mant = [round(x / (2 ** exp) * 127) for x in block]
print("block:", block, "shared exp:", exp)
print("mantissas:", mant)
